newsitem.title: USA: U.S. balloonist drops altitude in face of storm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist drops altitude in face of storm.

text.p: U.S. balloonist Steve Fossett dropped altitude to evade a thunderstorm on Sunday, but another storm front may force the global traveller to end his journey in India, his project manager said.

Fossett descended to 700 feet (213 metres) above ground from 18,300 feet (5,578 metres) earlier in the night. At 6:40 p.m. EST (2340 GMT), he was travelling over Varanasi, India, halfway between Calcutta and Delhi, at a highly reduced speed of 10 mph (16 kph), down from a speed of 65 mph (105 kph) earlier in the day, his support team reported.

"A thunderstorm is the last thing he wants to be in. But the decision will be his, whether to come down or ride it out," Bo Kemper, project manager, told Reuters from control headquarters at Loyola University of Chicago.
Kemper said either a sunrise or sunset landing would be the most practical. So far, no site has been chosen.
Though the balloon has three days' worth of fuel, any chance of a Pacific crossing is "slim," Kemper added. But continuing the unprecedented journey to Bangladesh remained a possibility.
The commodity broker-turned-adventurer was pressing on to topple the six-day plus 16 minute endurance record for a balloon flight, and could yet land in Bangladesh.
To do so, Fossett must remain aloft until 12:02 a.m. EST (0502 GMT), though his tracking crew said he may try to stretch the airborne time by a few hours past that target.
"He's cold and tired but in good spirits and happy to be physically well," said Frank Hartmann, assistant project manager.
The endurance record was set in 1981 by Americans Ben Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.

Fossett, who took off from Busch Stadium in St. Louis. on Monday, broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 5,435 miles (8,747 km) over Algeria on Friday. He set the earlier mark on a voyage from South Korea to Canada.
Doug Blount, a support team member, said travelling beyond Bangladesh would bring Fossett's 150-foot (45 metre) double-skinned balloon over south China, where flying permission remained unresolved.
Earlier in the journey political problems over the use of Libyan air space cost Fossett the around-the-world bid.

Although Libya later relented and Fossett's "Solo Spirit" cut across the southeastern tip of the country, his forced change of route cost him fuel he planned on using to cross the Pacific back to the United States, as well as putting him in a slower wind pattern.
